description: I’m passionate about astronomy, planets, and the mysteries of space. My strengths are writing, communication, storytelling, and creative thinking. I love combining science with art and finding engaging ways to present complex ideas. For PlanetX and SphereX, I’m looking for curious, creative teammates with skills in astronomy, coding, data analysis, science, visual design, or multimedia. Let’s turn curiosity into something meaningful!
summary:
Silent Sentinels is a mobile-first interactive storytelling web app created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, honoring NASA's abandoned explorers on the Moon and Mars. Built on a dark cosmic aesthetic (#0B0D17) with silver-cyan lunar and rust-orange Martian accents, Space Grotesk & Inter typography, and a live starfield canvas, it delivers an immersive, award-caliber experience.

The journey begins with a kinetic hero featuring a masked line-by-line title reveal and a parallax Moon disc. Visitors switch between THE MOON and MARS via an animated toggle showing key stats (70+ lunar artifacts since 1959; 20+ Martian spacecraft since 1971), then explore an interactive surface map where glowing pins mark real landing sites. Each pin opens a first-person story log — the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor 3, Opportunity, and Ingenuity — served from MongoDB through a FastAPI backend. Every card includes a browser-based "Play Audio Log" narration (Web Speech API with voice and speed controls) and a "View on NASA Trek" link. A telemetry marquee and an Artemis Accords heritage footer complete the archive — because abandoned never means forgotten.
details:
Project Details — Silent Sentinels: Echoes from the Moon & Mars

How it works

The app is a full-stack application with three layers:

Data layer (MongoDB): All four artifact stories (Apollo 15 LRV, Surveyor 3 & Apollo 12, Opportunity, Ingenuity), planet statistics, and landing-site coordinates are stored as structured documents. The database seeds itself automatically on first run — no manual setup needed.

Backend (FastAPI, Python): An API server exposes clean endpoints (/api/artifacts, /api/planets, /api/surfaces) that filter, sort, and serve the archive to any client. This means new rovers or artifacts can be added later without touching the interface.

Frontend (React): The interactive experience fetches the archive, renders the planet toggle with live stats, and maps each artifact's coordinates to glowing pins on a real satellite-imagery surface. Clicking a pin opens the story modal with the artifact's first-person monologue. The "Play Audio Log" button uses the browser's native Web Speech API — no external services — with playback speed (0.75x–1.5x) and voice selection controls.

Tools, languages & hardware

Languages: JavaScript (React), Python (FastAPI), HTML/CSS, MongoDB query language

Libraries: Framer Motion (animations), Lenis (smooth momentum scrolling), Tailwind CSS (styling), Motor (async database driver)

Software/AI tools: Canvas API (procedural starfield), Web Speech API (narration), generative AI imagery for the Mars helicopter visual, curated NASA-style photography

Hardware: None required — it runs entirely in any modern browser, desktop or phone, with no special devices or installations

Benefits

Emotional connection to science: First-person machine voices turn cold hardware into living witnesses, making planetary science memorable for students and the public

Heritage awareness: It directly supports the Artemis Accords' principle of preserving historic landing sites — the first interactive archive dedicated to "space heritage"

Fully accessible & free: No logins, no API keys, no costs to users; works on any device with graceful fallbacks if a browser lacks speech synthesis

Extensible: The database-driven design means the archive can grow to every discarded artifact on both worlds

Creativity

The signature idea is letting the machines speak. Instead of describing rovers in third person, each artifact narrates its own final days — "My battery is low and it's getting dark." Creative execution includes a kinetic masked-reveal hero, a Moon↔Mars theme system where the entire color palette shifts per planet, radar-ping pins over orbital imagery, a scanning telemetry overlay, and a slow editorial marquee of mission call-signs — all wrapped in a cinematic deep-space aesthetic.

Factors considered

Mobile-first design: Every section was built and verified at 390px before desktop, since most Space Apps judges browse on phones

Historical accuracy: All dates, coordinates, statuses, and quotes are presented exactly as recorded — no invented facts

Accessibility: WCAG-contrast text, keyboard-focusable controls, reduced-motion support for users with vestibular sensitivity

Performance: Lazy-loaded imagery, an optimized canvas starfield, and smooth 60fps scrolling even on mid-range phones

Reliability: Idempotent data seeding (no duplicate stories on restart), safe API error handling, and a resilient UI that never blanks on failure
